nameStory: The Great Black-backed Gull gets its name from being the largest gull species and having a distinctive dark blackish-grey back and wings that appear almost black from a distance. The 'great' in its name emphasizes its impressive size compared to other gulls, making it the giant of the gull family.
description: The Great Black-backed Gull is the largest member of the gull and tern family, a impressive seabird that commands attention along New England's coastlines. Adults have crisp white heads, necks, and bellies contrasting sharply with dark blackish-grey wings and backs, plus bright pink legs and yellow bills marked with a red spot. These powerful birds are aggressive hunters, pirates, and scavengers that will steal food from other seabirds and hunt everything from fish to small mammals. Their size and bold behavior make them easy to spot among flocks of smaller gulls.

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Noticeably larger and more robust than other gulls, with a thick neck and heavy, barrel-chested appearance that makes it stand out in mixed flocks

idTips.label: Back Color
idTips.description: Dark blackish-grey back and wings that appear almost black from a distance, much darker than the pale grey of Herring Gulls

idTips.label: Bill
idTips.description: Large, thick yellow bill with a distinctive red spot near the tip that looks like a drop of blood when viewed up close

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Bright pink legs that are thick and sturdy, noticeably pinker than the yellowish or pale pink legs of most other gulls

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Large, blocky white head with a fierce expression created by relatively small eyes set in the massive skull

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Powerful, steady flight with slower wingbeats than smaller gulls, often soaring with wings held slightly bent

habitat: Great Black-backed Gulls frequent New England's rocky coastlines, harbors, beaches, and offshore islands where they nest on cliffs and rocky ledges. They're commonly seen around fishing ports, landfills near the coast, and large bodies of water including coastal ponds and major rivers. During winter, some individuals move to large inland lakes and reservoirs, but they're most reliably found within sight of salt water.

seasonality.spring: Adults return to breeding areas with fully developed adult plumage, displaying territorial behavior around nesting sites on islands and coastal cliffs.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season when adults are most aggressive and protective, with chicks and juveniles visible by late summer showing mottled brown plumage.
seasonality.fall: Mixed flocks include adults and juveniles in various stages of molt, with some northern populations beginning to move south.
seasonality.winter: Most visible season as northern birds join year-round residents, congregating around harbors, dumps, and ice-free waters in impressive numbers.

funFact: Great Black-backed Gulls are such skilled pirates that they've been observed grabbing other seabirds by the tail and shaking them upside-down in mid-air until they vomit up their catch, which the gull then swoops down to steal before it hits the water.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Lesser Black-backed Gulls, but Great Black-backed Gulls are noticeably larger with darker, more blackish backs (versus slate-grey), and have pink legs instead of yellow. Remember: 'Great' means bigger and blacker, 'Lesser' means smaller with yellow legs.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their intimidating reputation, Great Black-backed Gulls were once much rarer in New England due to hunting pressure in the early 1900s, but have made a remarkable comeback and are now common year-round residents that some consider too successful for their own good.
compareHints: Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills. The massive size, dark back, and pink legs make Great Black-backed Gulls unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle.
Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs.
Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller.
Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression.
Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust.
Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip.
Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
